intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

units.title: Tectonic Forces
units.intro:
The Earth’s outer shell (the lithosphere) is broken into rigid **plates** that creep on the softer asthenosphere. Almost every large mountain, rift, volcano chain and earthquake belt sits on a plate edge. Internal heat drives the motion; we only see the results at the surface.

There are three relative motions. Name the motion first, then the landform — that is the safe exam pattern.

cards.title: 1.1 Tectonic Plates
body: The earth consists of a rigid outer layer called the lithosphere.
About 250 million years ago, there was a single super continent called Pangaea surrounded by a single super ocean known as Panthalassa.
About 210 million years ago Pangaea split into two land masses called Gondwanaland and Laurasia.

The splitting continued and in the northern hemisphere Laurasia split into North America and Eurasia (Europe and Asia) while in the southern hemisphere Gondwanaland broke into Africa, South America, Antarctica, India, Australia, New Zealand and Madagascar.
Subsequently, India separated from the Gondwanaland, moved further away and crashed into Asia.

cards.title: Divergent boundaries — plates pull apart
body: As two plates separate, magma rises and freezes into new crust. On a continent the crust first sags into a **rift valley** (East African Rift, the Afar / Danakil area). If rifting continues, the valley floods and becomes a narrow sea — that is the story of the **Red Sea**. In the open ocean the same process builds a mid-ocean ridge. Earthquakes here are usually shallow; volcanoes are common because the crust is thin.

cards.title: Convergent boundaries — plates meet
body: If one plate is oceanic, it is denser and **subducts** (dives) under the other. The diving slab melts; magma rises as a volcanic arc. A deep ocean trench marks the dive. If two continents meet, neither sinks easily — sediments crumple into **fold mountains** (think of a rug pushed across a floor). These collisions give the biggest ranges and deep earthquakes.

cards.title: Transform boundaries — plates slide past
body: Crust is neither created nor destroyed. Stress builds, then slips: earthquakes, offset rivers and fences, few volcanoes. Useful contrast question: “Why few volcanoes on a transform fault?” Because there is no melting slab and no gap for magma.

cards.title: Landforms built from inside
body:
- **Fold mountains** — compression wrinkles layered rock.
- **Block / fault mountains** — tension or shear snaps the crust; a block drops (graben) or is left standing (horst). Rift shoulders work this way.
- **Volcanoes** — magma reaches the surface at rifts and subduction zones.
- **Earthquakes** — sudden slip on a fault; energy travels as waves.

cards.title: Mnemonic — D.C.T.
body: Diverge = Divide (new crust, rift, Red Sea). Converge = Crash (trench or fold mountains). Transform = Slide (quakes, little lava). For Eritrea always add: “Our sea and Danakil sit on a divergent / rift setting.”

cards.title: How to write a tectonic paragraph
body: A 6-mark answer is usually: (1) name the boundary, (2) say what the plates do, (3) say what happens to crust / magma, (4) name the landform, (5) locate an example. Example: “The Red Sea is a divergent boundary. The African and Arabian plates are moving apart. Magma rises and new oceanic crust forms. The land first rifted, then flooded. That is why Eritrea has a young sea and a hot depression at Danakil.”

cards.title: How to write a tectonic paragraph
body: Volcanoes are not random. They cluster at rifts (thin crust) and at subduction zones (melting slab). Hot spots (e.g. a plume under a plate) are the exception the book may mention only in passing — don’t spend the essay there unless asked.

Earthquakes: focus = underground slip point; epicentre = the place on the surface above it. Shallow quakes at rifts and transforms; a mix of depths at subduction. Damage depends on magnitude, depth, rock type and building quality — a geography paper still wants the plate cause first.

cards.title: 1.3 Folding
body: When plates move towards each other and collide, the compressive forces that are created make the rock layers bend up and down.
Subsequently, the shape of the resulting land form looks like corrugated iron.
The process of bending of layers of the earth’s crust is called folding, and the resultant land forms are known as folds.
Folding occurs in sedimentary rock layers because sedimentary rocks are soft rocks that bend easily.
Depending on the intensity and direction of the compressive forces applied to the rock layers, different types of folds are created.

cards.title: Revision checklist (say these out loud)

cards.title: 1.4.1 Normal fault
body: Normal fault is formed where there is tensional force.
The Rift valley and block mountains are examples of land forms formed where normal faults occur.

cards.title: 1.4.2 Reverse fault
body: A reverse fault is formed by compressional forces.
The weight of the portion of the raised block hanging over the other block can be so high that it can lead to a force that causes the block to break off.

cards.title: 1.4.3 Tear fault
body: In a tear fault, the block of the earth’s crust moves in a horizontal direction, one side sliding past the other along the fault line.
The existence of the tear fault can be observed when looking at a river.
In such a case, the river turns at right angle at the fault and flows along the fault line for a short distance before it turns to its original direction.
A tear fault does not have a fault scrap because no block is raised or slipped down.

cards.title: 1.5.1 The damage earthquakes cause
body: The amount of damage caused by an earthquake depends on its magnitude.
5 or more on the Richter Scale cause loss of life, injury and major damage to property particularly when high rise buildings, highways and bridges collapse.
The damage is worsened by the disruption of essential services like water and power supply, transport, and the damage caused by fire started by exposed electric wires and leakage from gas pipes.
One day in 2003 an earthquake struck before dawn and destroyed most of the ancient Silk Road of Bam.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Distribution of earthquakes in the world
body: Japan, Indonesia and the west coast of North and South America experience a number of severe earthquakes (See fig. 1.15).

cards.title: 1.6.1 What is a volcano?
body: Volcanism is the process by which magma (molten rock materials) moves through the cracks of the earth’s crust until it reaches the surface and solidifies to form hard rocks.
All volcanoes are thus formed by the accumulation of lava and are generally conical in shape.
The magma, which forms deep in the earth, erupts through vents or long cracks called fissures.
The rising magma does not reach the surface in a regular manner.

cards.title: 1.6.2 Types of volcanic activity
body: The major land forms formed by extrusive volcanic activities are composite cone, cinder cone and shield volcanoes as well as calderas and lava plateaus.
Composite volcanoes: Composite volcanoes are composed of explosively erupted fragmental materials covered with nonexplosively erupted lava flows and other volcanic materials.
Shield volcanoes (volcanic shields): are roundish, moundlike volcanoes with gentle slopes constructed mainly of many fluid basaltic lava flows that erupt nonexplosively.
Cinder cone: A cinder cone is a small volcanic mountain formed by the accumulation of mainly cinders (rock pieces) ejected during explosive volcanic eruptions.

cards.title: 1.6.3 Distribution of volcanoes
body: Most earthquakes also occur along these boundaries, an indication of the close connection between plate boundaries, earthquakes, and volcanic activities.
The main areas of volcanoes and earthquakes are the Pacific ring of fire, the Alpine-Himalayan Belt, and the Mid-Atlantic Oceanic Ridge (See fig. 1.15).

cards.title: 1.6.4 Effects of volcanoes on humans
body: Volcanic activities have both negative and positive effects on peoples’ lives.
Volcanic ash clouds also disrupt air transport.

Yet their positive effects include the beautiful features produced are important sources of recreation and tourism, the fertile soil that results when the lava has weathered, and the production of geothermal energy from hot springs and geysers.

tips.text: Hundreds of millions years ago there was a single continent. This single continent first split into two huge land masses - Laurasia and Gondwanaland.
Subsequently, these land masses further split to form the tectonic plates or crustal plates.
The tectonic plates are in constant motion due to the convection currents created by the magma in the mantle.
The boundaries along which the plates move are of three types. They are divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries.
In a divergent boundary, two palates move away from each other, while a convergent boundary is a boundary where two plates collide against each other.
A transform boundary is where two plates slide horizontally past one another.

The movements are the cause for the drifting of the continents as well as the formation of the fold mountains, different kinds of faults, rift valleys, block mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes along the plate boundaries.
This is why the location of the concentration of earthquakes, volcanoes and unstable areas of the world are the same.

units.title: Gradation by Rivers and Winds
units.intro: **Gradation** is the slow flattening of the land: high places are worn down (*degradation*) and low places are filled (*aggradation*). Agents: rivers, wind, waves (Unit 3), ice (less relevant here), and gravity (mass wasting). Tectonics builds; gradation sculpts.

f1.title: A river grows old as the slope dies. Wadis in Eritrea often only run after rain — same three jobs, less water.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Degradation force
body: Degradation (Denudation) is the lowering of land by weathering and erosion due to the action of sun, rain, wind, rivers, frost and ice.
The change that comes on the surface of the rock due to the change of weather is called weathering.
In other words, weathering is the breaking down of hard rocks due to change of weather.
Physical weathering (mechanical weathering) is the breaking down and disintegration of rocks by many factors such as temperature changes, physical action of water, animals and plants.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Aggradation
body: Aggradation (Deposition) is the raising of the height of land by the deposition of the weathered and eroded materials.
After a long period of consolidation, these sediments can form sedimentary rocks.

cards.title: 2.2.1 What is a rRiver?
body: A river is a flow of water in a natural channel.
Most rivers begin flowing from wet mountains, springs, lakes or melting snow.
The point where a river begins is called a river source.
At the river source, the river water flows in a tiny and narrow channel called a rill.

cards.title: 2.2.2 The work of a river
body: First, it erodes the land in a particular place.
Second, it deposits the eroded materials in other places.
Weathered materials due to physical weathering chemical weathering are is accumulated at the base of the parent rocks or hills.
The process of the washing away of the weathered material is called sheet erosion.

cards.title: How a river works
body: A river has three jobs that happen together but dominate in different stretches.

1. **Erosion** — hydraulic action (the force of the water), abrasion (load scrapes the bed), attrition (stones smash each other smaller), solution (soluble rock dissolves).
2. **Transport** — dissolved load, suspended mud, saltation of sand, traction of cobbles along the bed. Faster, fuller rivers carry more and coarser load.
3. **Deposition** — when speed falls (inside of a bend, mouth, flood plain) the heaviest pieces drop first.

cards.title: A river grows old as the slope dies. Wadis in Eritrea often only run after rain — same three jobs, less water.
How a river works
body: **Upper course** (steep highland): vertical erosion, V-shaped valleys, interlocking spurs, potholes, waterfalls where hard rock sits over soft.

**Middle course:** lateral erosion starts to win. The channel swings into **meanders**. The outer bank is undercut (river cliff); the inner bank grows a point bar. A big flood may cut the neck and leave an ox-bow.

**Lower course:** gradient tiny, huge load of silt. Flood plain, levées, braided reaches, delta or estuary at the sea. Many Eritrean streams never reach a quiet old age — they are seasonal **wadis**: violent after rain, dry beds the rest of the year. Same three processes, pulsed.

**Wind** needs dry, loose sediment and weak plant cover — so it dominates semi-desert and desert. *Deflation* lifts fines and leaves a stony pavement. *Abrasion* sands the rock into yardangs and polished faces. Deposition builds dunes (shape depends on wind direction and sand supply) and can dump fine dust as loess far downwind. After overgrazing, wind finds more to eat — link this to Unit 5.

cards.title: Factors that decide how hard a river works
body: Volume (more rain or a bigger catchment), gradient (steeper = more energy), rock hardness, load already being carried, and vegetation on the banks. After a rare cloudburst a small Eritrean wadi can shift more gravel in one night than in the following six dry months. That is why bridges get wrecked and why farmers farm the wet bed anyway — the silt is a gift and a risk.

cards.title: 2.4.1 What is the work of wind
body: Winds have tremendous force to cut off branches of trees and remove weathered materials from the surface of the earth.
The role of wind in changing the earth’s surface is more dominant in dry areas such as hot deserts and semi-deserts.
Deserts are also covered with rock waste that is produced by weathering of solid rocks.
Eventually, a surface layer of closely packed stone called a desert pavement is formed as the sand and silt are removed.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Features produced by wind erosion
body: The erosive work of winds depends on the quantity of sand particles the wind carries and the speed of the wind.
For example, strong winds can drive sand particles with a tremendous force against standing rocks for several kilometres.
The major noticeable features produced by wind action are as follows.
The top of the upstanding rock remains undisturbed and the lower portion is changed into a thin pillar.

cards.title: 2.4.3 Features produced by wind deposition

tips.text: Nothing that we see is permanent Tectonic forces increase the height of the surface of the earth. These are internal forces that originate from the interior of the earth. There are also external forces that reduce the heights of mountains, plateaus and hills.
These are accomplished by rivers, winds, wave actions, and glacial actions. These elements of external forces reduce the surface of the earth by wearing and erosion.
The external forces that change the surface of the earth is associated with erosion. These external forces that raise or lower the level lands are collectively called gradational forces.
Gradational force has two parts, namely, degradation and aggradation.
Degradation is the lowering away of land by weathering and erosion.
Aggradation is the increase of the height of land by deposition.
Rivers and winds modify the earth’s surface by eroding, transporting, and depositing the eroded materials. Both rivers and winds have features produced by their erosive action and deposition action.
The course of a river is divided into three stages. These are the upper course (steep-sided course), middle course (gentle slope), and lower course (flat land).
The action of the river in the three stages varies.
In the upper course, the action is erosion and transporting the eroded materials.

units.title: Gradation by The Action of Waves
units.intro:
Waves are wind energy delivered to a coastline. When they break, they throw water and stones at the cliff (**hydraulic action + abrasion**). A weakness becomes a notch, then a cave. If caves meet through a headland you get an **arch**. When the roof falls you have a **stack**; the stack wears to a **stump**.

Where waves lose energy they deposit: beaches (sorted sand/shingle), spits across a bay mouth, tombolos joining an island. Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast in the direction of the prevailing wave approach.

The wind blowing over a smooth surface of water creates small ripples (small wave or series of tiny waves) that grow into recognizable waves.
If the wind continues to blow for several hours, the height of the waves increase.
A wind blowing about 50 kilometers per hour for 30 hours over the open sea will raise waves about 6 meters high.

units.title: Human Settlement
units.intro:
A **settlement** is a place people occupy with some permanence — a seasonal camp, a village, a town, a city. Geography asks *where* and *why there*, then *what the place does*.

**Site** is the exact piece of ground: a spring, a dry point above a marsh, a hill for defence, a bridging point, a sheltered harbour, a mining outcrop. Site answers “why this plot?”

cards.title: 4.1 What is Settlement?
body: A settlement is a place where people come to build their houses and live.
Settlements are the expressions of human occupancy of the earth’s surface.
Settlements are purposefully organized clusters of houses and non-residential buildings.
Settlements reflect the relationship of human beings with their environment.
Settlements also reflect the social, economic, and cultural aspects of society.

cards.title: Rural Settlements
body: **Situation** is the place in the wider network: on a highland–port road, in the middle of a farming basin, at a border. Situation answers “why this plot stayed important when weapons or wetlands changed.” A good harbour (site) that sits on a world shipping lane (situation) becomes a city; a good harbour at the end of nowhere may stay a village.

**Functions** change through time. A place may start as a market, add administration, then industry or a port. Most real towns are multi-functional; the exam still wants you to name the *dominant* one and a piece of evidence (docks, ministries, factories, shrine).

**Rural settlements** in Eritrea include highland farming villages and lowland pastoral / agro-pastoral camps. Pattern may be nucleated (clustered around water or a church/mosque) or dispersed (farmsteads in fields).

cards.title: 4.2.1 Basic factors that determine the site of rural settlements
body: The needs for space by human beings are of primary importance for human settlements.
A place that presents these requirements provides an ideal site for settlement.
The environment provides the site, building materials, and other resources like water that may influence the location of settlements in general.
Factors that influence the location or site of rural settlements are directly related to the livelihood systems of rural people.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Types and patterns of rural settlements
body: Rural settlements vary in type, distribution, pattern, size, shape, and other characteristics due to various physical and cultural (human) factors.
The distribution and pattern of rural settlements can be approached in two ways.
Rural settlements can be classified into three types on the basis of size.
Isolated buildings emerge when farmers build their shelter on their farms at a distance from the nearest village or hamlet.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Classification of rural settlements
body: One classification is on the basis of permanence of the settlement.
Ephemeral, if they last 1-7 days in a particular place. b.
Temporary, if they last 1-30 days in a place. c.
Seasonal, if they last several months in a place. d.

cards.title: 4.2.4 Function of rural settlements
body: Settlements are created to satisfy economic, social, political technological and cultural needs of people.
Over time they may assume additional functions.
Settlements develop through a continuous process and require continuous investment.
The importance of every settlement largely depends on its location or position within the whole system of settlements.

cards.title: 4.2.5 Evolution of rural settlements
body: Up to about 13, 000 B.C.E., people depended on hunting and gathering for their living.
After this, which was also the end of the Ice Age, changing environmental and demographic conditions caused major changes in the hunter-gatherer societies.
Technological improvements led to sedentary settlements in areas that had abundant and seasonally predictable food resources.
Domestication of plants and animals started in various parts of the world.

cards.title: 4.2.6 Place names
body: Settlements, whether urban or rural, are identified by names.
The study of the origins and meaning of place names is called toponymy.
Place names are the product of ecological diversity, cultural perception, and wealth of places.
Place names are helpful in establishing relationships between different regions or even within the same region.

cards.title: Urban Settlements
body: **Urban growth:** trade, colonial administration, industry, and rural–urban migration. In many developing countries the built-up area and informal housing race ahead of piped water, jobs and formal titles. In richer cities the story is often suburban sprawl plus later attempts to revive the old centre.

cards.title: 4.3.1 The Nature of urban settlements
body: Cities are among the oldest marks of civilization.
Since their first appearance 4000 to 6000 years ago, they have continued to emerge and grow or die.
Cities are part of a larger, urban and rural society and economy.
Cities show an orderly internal arrangement of land uses, social groups, and economic functions.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Factors of town location
body: For a town to perform its functions, it must be located at a suitable position.
Centrality, good transport facility, resource availability, flat terrain, and other factores encourage the growth of urban settlements.
Site refers to the actual physical quality of the place a town or city occupies.
Terrain features of the place on which a city is located and its absolute location are the two basic site features.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Functions of towns
body: Towns, irrespective of their size, age or location, exist to perform certain functions that cannot be carried out in dispersed locations.
Usually, towns that have a larger number of different kinds of functions grow very fast and become large in size.
Manufacturing: These are towns mainly engaged in the manufacturing of goods.
Pittsburgh, Detroit and Michigan in the USA and Tokyo in Japan are manufacturing cities.

cards.title: 4.3.4 Emergence and growth of urban settlements
body: The emergence of sedentary agriculture led to fixed settlements, but for many years, settlements remained truly rural.
The emergence of specialised segments of society (farmers, artisans, soldiers, merchants, elites, and others) gave to the need for new political systems.
Groups of settlements came under one central authority.

Later this process spread to other places like the Nile delta, Indus valley, Mediterranean Europe, Mesoamerica, and other places The emergence of central authority and the need to administer territories from a single location gave rise to the emergence of towns.

cards.title: 4.3.5 Cities in developing countries
body: With increasing population, the area occupied by towns and cities increases.
As cities expand, thousands of hectares of agricultural land is used for non-agricultural purposes thereby decreasing food production.
The growth of housing in many towns of the less developed countries is much slower than their population growth.
Many cities like Nairobi, Jakarta, Mexico City and Cairo are surrounded by densely populated slums and shantytowns.

cards.title: 4.3.6 Cities in developed dountries
body: One of the major problems faced by such cities is traffic congestion.
Beijing has over three million cars, and driving in such towns is extremely difficult and time consuming.
Traffic congestion is particularly high during rush hours when the roads are crowded with taxis, private cars and buses.
The presence of too many cars and industries means too much pollution.

units.title: Cultural Impact on the Natural Environment
units.intro:
Culture here means how people use the land: farming, herding, cutting wood, building cities, burning fuel. The physical environment offers limits (rain, slope, soil); culture can respect those limits or push them until the system snaps.

**Deforestation.** Trees are cut for fuel, construction, charcoal and new fields. Without roots and canopy, rain hits bare soil, runoff rises, rivers silt, springs weaken, local climate gets harsher. In Eritrea this is tightly tied to energy poverty (Unit 12 Ag / Geo 12 forests).

cards.title: 5.1 Understanding the Natural Environment
body: Human beings exist within a specific environment, which they have modified through activities such clearing of forests, building of roads and settlements.
Ancient people had very limited effects on the natural environment.
With the development of agriculture and industry, changes on the environment increased rapidly.
Modern technology has changed the relationships between people and their natural surroundings.
The most significant of these are the growth in world population and advancement in modern technology.

cards.title: Humans as Modifiers of the Natural Environment
body: **Desertification.** Productive dryland loses vegetation and soil until it behaves like desert. Causes are usually mixed: drought + too many animals on the same range + ploughing fragile soil + tree cutting. It is not a simple “desert advancing like a wall”. Reversing it means rest (enclosures), controlled grazing, and putting cover back.

**Global warming.** Extra greenhouse gases (CO₂ from fossil fuel and from lost forest, methane from livestock and waste) trap more outgoing heat. Effects that matter locally: more erratic rain, hotter lowlands, stress on already marginal farms.

**Acid rain and air pollution.** Sulphur and nitrogen oxides from industry and vehicles dissolve in rain and damage plants, water and stone. Cities add smoke, dust and traffic fumes. Even without giant factories, charcoal and diesel can foul a valley.

cards.title: Exam habit
body: Always pair a human cause with a physical result: “overgrazing → bare soil → wind/water erosion → lower yields.” One-word answers (“pollution”) score poorly.

cards.title: Who is most exposed?
body: Pastoral lowlands feel drought and desertification first. Highland slopes feel deforestation as gullies. Coastal towns feel heat, salt and any sea-level talk. A good essay names a belt, a process, and one practical response already in later books: terrace, enclosure, stove that uses less wood, managed grazing.

cards.title: 6.1 Location
body: The relative location of Eritrea with respect to its neighboring, countries, water bodies and land masses.
The location of Eritrea can be expressed both in terms of the absolute and relative locations.
The absolute location is based on mathematical values, arc of circle, as well as imaginary lines of latitudes and longitudes.
The relative location of a place is determined by its location in relation to its nearby land masses and water bodies.
In terms of latitude, Eritrea extends from 12°42’ N (on the Djibouti border) to 18°02 N (Ras Kassar on the Sudan border).

cards.title: Where, how big, why it matters
body: Eritrea sits on the northern Horn of Africa, with a long **Red Sea** frontage. Neighbours: Sudan (west), Ethiopia (south), Djibouti (south-east). Latitude is tropical, so lowlands are hot; the plateau is liveable because **altitude** lowers temperature. Always mention both latitude and altitude when you explain climate here.

cards.title: 6.2 Administration
body: The six administrative zones are divided into 59 sub-zones.
All the remaining zones except the Southern Red Sea have common boundaries with it.
Asmara, the capital city of Eritrea is also found in this zone.
Five zones have common boundaries either with Sudan or Ethiopia.

cards.title: 6.3 The Size and Shape of Eritrea
body: Eritrea has a total area of 124,330 square kilometers.
Eritrea also possesses over 360 islands, which have a total coastline of over 1258.4 kilometers.
The islands can be generally classified into small or large islands on the basis of the total area they occupy.
Small islands occupy less than 10 square kilometer each.
The largest island is called Dahlak Kebir (Table.6.2).

cards.title: Where, how big, why it matters
body: The country is elongated roughly north–south, thin in places, with the Dahlak waters and a southern Red Sea reach. That shape gives a long coast relative to land area — useful for ports and fisheries, awkward for east–west roads that must climb the escarpment.

cards.title: 6.4 Strategic Position of Eritrea
body: The geographical location of a country, which is expressed through its absolute and relative locations, is closely associated with the country’s natural resources endowments as well.
The strategic position of the country is. therefore. best explained in relation to its relative and absolute geographical locations.
Eritrea is not far from the equatorial location.
The Eritrean Red Sea coast stretches for about 1216 kilometers along the western shore of the Red Sea.
Most commercial lines directed to Europe and the Mediterranean regions from the Persian Gulf, East Africa and Asia pass through the Red Sea.

cards.title: Where, how big, why it matters
body: **Strategic position:** the Red Sea is a world shortcut between the Mediterranean / Suez and the Indian Ocean. A state that can offer a safe port on that lane has diplomatic and commercial weight out of proportion to its land size. Internally the Massawa–Asmara corridor ties the sea to the populated highlands. Assab sits further south on the same sea.

cards.title: Relief — five belts to be able to sketch
body:
1. **Western lowlands** — broad, hot, falling toward Sudan. Sorghum / pastoral country; rivers like Barka and Gash.
2. **Highlands** — the spine. Cooler, more densely settled, rain-fed cereals. Asmara sits here.
3. **Eastern escarpment** — a steep drop toward the sea. Orographic moisture can make this the greenest strip; roads zigzag.
4. **Coastal plain** — narrow, hot, humid to arid depending on stretch; Massawa and the ports.
5. **Danakil / southern depression** — below or near sea level in parts, extreme heat, salt, rift geology (tie back to Unit 1).

body: The rivers Haddas, Comayli, Endeli, Dandero, Alighede and Labka have cut deep valleys.
The Escarpment is varied and so fascinating.
The part of the Eastern Escarpment, locally known as Bahri, is highly vegetated.
The lowest elevation is about 500m.a.s.l. but it rises sharply to the upper edge.

cards.title: 7.1.3 The highlands
body: The highlands of Eritrea occupy the central portion of the country extending from south to north.
The highlands are divided into six land features.
Hager Nues being 2770m.a.s.l. is the highest peak in this highland region.

cards.title: Tap-level sketch (same idea as Grade 12). East drainage to the Red Sea; west to Sudan; some streams die in Danakil.
Drainage — three stories, not one national river
body: **Eastern system:** short, steep catchments racing down the escarpment to the Red Sea. Flashy after rain; little room for long flood plains.
**Western system:** longer rivers (Barka, Anseba, Gash–Mereb, Setit on the border) that drain toward Sudan. More useful for alluvial farming where the bed is wide, still seasonal.
**Danakil interior:** some streams never reach the sea; they evaporate or sink in the depression. Endorheic = closed basin.
Lakes in Eritrea are few and often seasonal or coastal / lagoonal rather than great inland seas. Do not invent a “Lake Victoria of Eritrea” on the paper.

cards.title: 7.3 Lakes in Eritrea

Lake Bordole is located in the Buri Peninsula where salt is extracted.
Lake Bada and Lake Aba Adad are found in the Danakil Depression.
All are salty lakes, which carry water during the rainy season and dry up during the dry season.

tips.text: The present relief of Eritrea is highly diversified and consists of different types of features that include mountain ranges, deep gorges, plains and offshore islands.
The country’s relief is broadly divided into three major divisions. These are the Highlands, the Lowlands and the Escarpments.
The Highlands extend from south to north.
The Northern Highlands are very much dissected by major river systems such as River Anseba.
The Central Plateau occupies geographically important location as major rivers of Eritrea originate from this plateau.

units.title: Map Work: Landforms on Contour Maps
units.intro:
A **contour line** joins every point that is the same height above a datum (usually sea level). The map does not show every metre — it samples at a fixed **contour interval** (e.g. 20 m). Read the printed numbers; never guess the interval.

**Spacing is slope.** Packed lines = you climb a lot in a short walk = steep (escarpment). Wide lines = gentle (western plains). A uniform spacing = even slope. Lines that suddenly pack after being wide = a break of slope (terrace edge, cliff).

cards.title: 8.1 Major Land forms on Maps
body: Hill: A hill is an area of land usually rounded in shape that is higher than the surrounding areas.
A hill has a broad base and is almost circular in shape.
Contours showing a conical hill are almost circular with peak of the hill at their center.
Contour lines representing a hill are drawn almost at regular distances.
The value of contour increases towards the centre (Fig. 8.1).

cards.title: 8.2 Minor Land forms on Maps
body: A single type of a major land form may contain one or more types of minor land forms.
A mountain ridge, for example, may include many other minor land features. due to external and internal forces.
Valley: A valley is a depressed area formed either by tectonic forces or the agents of weathering.
Depending on the nature and magnitude of such natural forces, valleys can attain either a V or a U-shaped pattern.
A V-shaped valley is formed by the erosion of a river.

cards.title: Minor Land forms on Maps
body: **Closed loop** with values rising toward the centre = hill or mountain. Closed loop with values falling toward the centre (sometimes marked with hachure ticks) = hollow or crater. Two loops sharing a saddle = col / pass — the usual road place across a ridge.

cards.title: 8.3 Gradients and Cross Sections
body: Gradient expresses the ratio of change in the altitude of a slope.
In other words, it expresses the ratio between vertical distance and horizontal distance.
The measurement of a gradient is used for the purpose of comparing the steepness of slopes more accurately.
To calculate the gradient between any two points on a contour map, two things must be known.
Knowledge of a gradient becomes very useful in the construction of roads and railways in mountainous areas.

cards.title: 8.4 Intervisibility
body: Two points A and B on the ground are said to be intervisible if point A can be seen from point B and point B can be seen from point A.

Intervisibility
body: **Valley vs spur.** Contours bend into a V. If the V points *upslope* (into the highland), you are looking at a valley — water runs out of the V. If the V points *downslope*, it is a spur standing out from the hill. Rivers are drawn along the valley V, never along the spur V.
**Gradient** = vertical rise ÷ horizontal distance (same units). Example: 100 m rise over 2 000 m run = 1/20 or 5%. On the map, measure the run with the scale; read the rise from contour numbers.
**Cross-section:** lay a paper edge on the map line, tick every contour with its height, transfer the ticks to graph paper, join the dots. That drawing is what “the land looks like along A–B.”

**Intervisibility:** can a person at A see a person at B? Draw the A–B section. If any ridge rises above the straight line of sight, they cannot see each other. Trees and buildings also block, but the textbook wants the landform reason first.

cards.title: Tricks that save marks
body: 1) V into the hill = valley. 2) Count the interval before you shout “steep”. 3) Gradient needs both rise and scale distance — height marks alone are not a gradient. 4) Intervisibility without a section is a guess.

cards.title: Revision checklist (say these out loud)
body: - Packed contours = steep. V into the hill = valley. Gradient = rise / run. Intervisibility needs a section.

tips.text: Geographers use different measurement techniques to classify the morphology or shape of the earth’s physical features.
Elevation, slope steepness are some of the common examples frequently used to classify land forms.
Others may apply only size as major distinguishing criterion. In this unit, the criteria used to identify land features are many.
In this measurement system, some land forms stand out distinctively from their surroundings, while other may be identified in association to distinct land forms.
Land forms that are widely distributed in many places are called major land forms.
Land forms whose presences are mostly linked with the major land forms are called minor land features.
Contour lines representing such land forms show different characteristics.
